2027-07-10.title: Saturday of the seventh week after Pentecost
readings: Have they stumbled so as to fall? By no means! If the root is holy, then the branches also are holy
Coming down from the mountain, Jesus heals the only son of a desperate father
2027-07-10.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Seventh Sunday after Pentecost. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam today.
2027-07-10.verse: If the part of the dough offered as first fruits is holy, then the whole batch is holy; and if the root is holy, then the branches also are holy.
theo: St Paul asks a question that he has clearly asked himself with tears: “So I ask, have they stumbled so as to fall? By no means!” He is speaking of his own people, the Jews, most of whom had not yet recognised Jesus as the Messiah. Paul had once said that he could wish himself cut off from Christ for the sake of his kindred (Romans 9:3), so this is no cold discussion. He answers that their stumbling is not the end of the story. “But through their stumbling salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous.” God can bring good even out of a stumble, and the good that came to the nations is meant to draw Israel back with a holy longing. “Now if their stumbling means riches for the world, and if their defeat means riches for Gentiles, how much more will their full inclusion mean!” Paul is looking ahead to a day of fullness. The Catechism says that the glorious coming of the Messiah awaits the recognition of him by all Israel, and that the Church looks to that day with the hope of the whole world (Catechism 674, in substance). Meanwhile the Church must never speak of the Jewish people as rejected: the Jewish covenant has never been revoked (Catechism 839–840, in substance).

Paul then turns to us, the Gentiles: “Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I glorify my ministry in order to make my own people jealous, and thus save some of them.” An apostle to the nations whose heart is still with his own people: this is the Paul we love. He adds, “For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead!” When God's whole plan is complete it will feel like a resurrection. Then he gives two pictures: “If the part of the dough offered as first fruits is holy, then the whole batch is holy; and if the root is holy, then the branches also are holy.” In the Law a cake from the first of the dough was set aside for God (Numbers 15:17–21), and the whole baking was blessed by it. The patriarchs and the faith of Israel are that first portion and that root. In the verses that follow Paul will say that we Gentiles are wild branches grafted onto the tree, and that the root bears us and not we the root (Romans 11:17–24). Every Qurbono shows this. We sing the psalms of David, we cry Alleluia, a Hebrew word, we read Moses and the prophets before the Gospel, and our whole prayer breathes the air of the Scriptures of Israel. The Church of St Thomas in India has always lived on that root.

The Gospel brings us down from the mountain. “On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him.” The day before, on the mountain, Peter, James and John had seen the glory of Jesus; now, in the valley, there is a father in anguish. “Teacher, I beg you to look at my son; he is my only child. Suddenly a spirit seizes him, and all at once he shrieks.” Luke notes, as he does for the widow's son at Nain and for Jairus's daughter, that it is an only child. “I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.” Jesus answers with a sigh that belongs to every teacher who has seen a lesson not understood: “You faithless and perverse generation, how much longer must I be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.” It is not a verdict on any one people; it is the sorrow of a master whose own disciples have not yet learned. Then, “While he was coming, the demon dashed him to the ground in convulsions. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, healed the boy, and gave him back to his father.” The boy has been thrown down, but he is raised and given back; the Lord, who had come down the mountain, takes hold of him. St Mark's longer account records the father's cry, “I believe; help my unbelief!” and says that the boy lay like a corpse until Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up (Mark 9:24, 26–27). Stumbling is not falling. As the psalm says, “though we stumble, we shall not fall headlong, for the Lord holds us by the hand.” And Luke ends: “And all were astounded at the greatness of God.” In the valley, where the sick are, there the greatness of God is seen.
outline: Ask: where in my life, or in my family, have I stumbled and thought I had fallen?
Paul's question about his own people; God brings good even from a stumble, and holds his people by the hand.
First fruits and root: the Church lives from the faith of Israel; no contempt, only gratitude.
The valley of the father and his only child: Jesus raises and gives back; the cry “I believe; help my unbelief!”
“If the root is holy, then the branches also are holy.”
live: This week, when you hear a psalm or an Alleluia at Holy Qurbono, thank God for the people of Israel through whom the Scriptures came.
Bring one person who is struggling, a sick relative, a worried friend, to Jesus in a specific prayer, and tell them you are praying.
Do not despair of a fall (Psalm 37:24)
If you have stumbled in a habit or a promise, go to confession and begin again; the Lord holds you by the hand.
2027-07-10.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you came down from the mountain to the valley of the suffering and gave the child back to his father. We thank you for the root from which we have been fed, the faith of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and the Scriptures of your people, and we ask you to hasten the day when all Israel will be saved and all the nations will be one in your love. When we stumble, hold us by the hand; when we cannot cast out our own evil, say to us, “Bring him here.” Heal the sick, comfort their parents, and make us glad to praise the greatness of God. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono we come down from the mountain of the Word to the table of the Lord; he takes the bread, as he took the boy by the hand, and gives us back, healed, to our Father.

quick: St Paul asks whether Israel has stumbled so as to fall, and answers: by no means; the gifts of God are not taken back.
If the root is holy, so are the branches: the Church lives from the root of Israel's faith and must never despise it.
Coming down from the mountain, Jesus heals a father's only son and gives him back to his father.
2027-07-10.action: Pray the Hail Mary today for a family that has a sick child, and say aloud one psalm of Israel.
2027-07-10.question: Where have I stumbled and believed that I had fallen, when the Lord was holding my hand?

family.explain: A father ran to Jesus because his only son was very ill, and the friends of Jesus could not help. Jesus said, “Bring your son here,” and he healed the boy and gave him back to his father. Jesus is never too busy for a child who is hurting, and he loves the parents who bring them. St Paul adds that we are like branches of a tree whose roots go back to Abraham, so we should love the Jewish people, who first received the Bible, and thank God for them.
family.intention: We pray for sick children and their parents, and for doctors and nurses, especially in the monsoon months when fevers spread.
family.ask: Ask: “Who do we know that needs to be brought to Jesus in prayer today?”

illus: A father from the hill country near Thodupuzha came to the church every Saturday carrying his grown son, who had been ill from childhood and could not walk. After the Qurbono the priest once asked him, gently, whether he still believed that his boy would be healed. The man thought for a while and said: Father, I do not know how much faith I have. I only know that I keep bringing him. In the Gospel the father brought his son, and Jesus did the rest. So I bring, and I leave the rest to him. The priest said afterwards that he had not heard a better sermon on the Gospel in all his years.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you take us by the hand when we stumble, and you give back what seemed lost. Hold us, heal us and make us thankful for the root from which we live. Amen.
share: Have they stumbled so as to fall? By no means! (Romans 11:11). When has a stumble in my life led to something good?
If the root is holy, then the branches also are holy (Romans 11:16). What do I owe to the faith of Israel and to the faith of my own grandparents?
Bring your son here (Luke 9:41). Whom could I bring to Jesus today?
pm.resp: Lord, hold us by the hand.
interc: For the Jewish people, beloved of God for the sake of their ancestors, and for friendship and understanding between Jews and Christians.
For parents with sick or disabled children, that they may be strengthened and find help.
For doctors, nurses and carers, especially in this season of fevers and floods.
For those who have stumbled in sin or failure, that they may rise and begin again.
For our parish, that we may be a place where all who suffer are brought to the Lord.
pm.close: Father, you hold your people by the hand even when they stumble. Make us grateful for the root that bears us, and bring us all, healed and forgiven, into the fullness of your kingdom. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, St Paul asks today: have they stumbled so as to fall? By no means! (Romans 11:11). He is speaking of his own people, whom he never stops loving. And he gives us a picture to hold on to: if the root is holy, then the branches also are holy (Romans 11:16). We are branches that have been grafted on, and the root is the faith of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the Scriptures of Israel, the psalms we sing at every Qurbono. So there is no room for pride, and no room for contempt, but only gratitude.

The Gospel brings us down from the mountain into the valley. A father cries out of the crowd: Teacher, I beg you to look at my son; he is my only child (Luke 9:38). His son is thrown to the ground again and again. The disciples tried and could not. And Jesus says, with a sigh: Bring your son here (Luke 9:41). Then he rebukes the unclean spirit, heals the boy, and gives him back to his father (Luke 9:42).

Do you see how much love there is in those words, gave him back to his father? Jesus does not heal the child and keep him; he returns him to his father's arms. There is not a single sorrow of a parent that he does not see. And when we ourselves have stumbled, when we feel that we have fallen for good, it is the same Lord who takes our hand: though we stumble, we shall not fall headlong, for the Lord holds us by the hand (Psalm 37:24).

So today let us bring someone to Jesus: a sick relative, a troubled friend, or ourselves. Let us say with the father in Mark's Gospel: I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24). And let us thank God for the root that bears us. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever fallen down while running and thought you could never get up? Then someone gave you a hand and you were up again. Today's Gospel is about a father whose little boy was very sick. The father brought his boy to Jesus, and Jesus made him well and gave him back to his father, safe and sound. Jesus always takes our hand when we fall. Also, St Paul tells us we are like branches of a big tree, and the roots of the tree are the people of the Bible, Abraham and Moses and David. We say thank you to them in our hearts. This week, when you fall or make a mistake, say: Jesus, hold my hand. And ask Jesus to help a child who is sick.

intro: Theme: “If the root is holy, then the branches also are holy.”
On Saturday of the seventh week after Pentecost: Paul's question about Israel, the root that bears the Church, and the father who brings his only son down from the mountain to Jesus.

So I ask, have they stumbled so as to fall? By no means!
points.apply: If you have fallen in a habit or a promise, go to confession this week and begin again.

sub: Wild branches grafted onto the tree.
The psalms and the Alleluia of every Qurbono.
q: and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.
For he is our peace; in his flesh he has made both groups into one and has broken down the dividing wall, that is, the hostility between us.
points.apply: Thank God for the people of Israel whenever you hear a psalm at the Qurbono, and speak of the Jewish people with respect.

sub: The glory on the mountain, the pain in the valley.
The only child, the disciples who could not.
Jesus raises the boy and gives him back to his father.
q: The Lord is near to the brokenhearted, and saves the crushed in spirit.
Immediately the father of the child cried out, “I believe; help my unbelief!”
points.apply: Bring one person in need to Jesus today in a prayer said aloud.

concl: The Lord does not let his people fall: the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable, and he holds us by the hand.
The Church lives from a holy root, and from the altar she is sent to the valleys where the suffering wait.
2027-07-10.resolve: Be grateful for the root, hold on to the Lord's hand, and bring someone in need to him.
